title: Pricing strategies
examples: When should a company use skimming over penetration?
Can cost-plus pricing work for a new product?
What is the difference between skimming and penetration?

explain.say: Today we are learning about pricing strategies. These are methods businesses use to set their prices. A price affects how many people will buy the product.

items: Pricing is how much something costs.
Strategies help businesses choose that price.

explain.say: Skimming pricing involves setting a high initial price. This is often done for new, innovative products. You capture early adopters who are willing to pay more.

draw.text: Skimming: High initial price, new products.

explain.say: Penetration pricing sets a low initial price to enter the market. This goal is to gain a large number of customers quickly. You aim to build market share fast.

draw.text: Penetration: Low initial price, high volume.

explain.say: Cost-plus pricing is straightforward and easy to calculate. You calculate the total cost and then add a fixed profit margin. This guarantees a set profit per item.
Imagine a brand new type of electric scooter. If you use skimming, you charge a lot to early tech enthusiasts. If you use penetration, you charge very little to get everyone to try it.
A common mistake is using skimming when the market is very sensitive to price. You might lose potential customers who cannot afford the high initial cost. Always research your target buyer first.

items: Always match price to perceived value.

faq.q: What is the main difference between skimming and penetration?
faq.a: Skimming starts high and drops later, targeting those who pay more initially. Penetration starts low to attract a large number of buyers quickly.
asks: When should I use high prices first?
Does penetration always mean low prices?

faq.q: Is cost-plus pricing always the best method?
faq.a: No, it ignores what customers are actually willing to pay. You must consider market demand, not just your costs.
asks: Should I only base price on my expenses?

faq.q: Do I have to choose only one strategy?
faq.a: Businesses can sometimes mix strategies, but they usually focus on one primary approach at launch. It depends on the product and market.
asks: Can I use both skimming and penetration?
Is it okay to change strategies later?

faq.q: Who is best suited for skimming pricing?
faq.a: Skimming works best for unique, patented, or highly innovative goods. These products offer clear value that people will pay a premium for.
asks: What kind of product fits skimming?
When is a high initial price acceptable?

faq.q: What does 'market share' mean in this context?
faq.a: Market share is the percentage of total sales in a specific market that your business captures. Low initial pricing aims to increase this share.
asks: What is the goal of penetration pricing?
How do I measure my market share?

facts: Skimming is effective when the product has little competition.
Penetration pricing is useful for non-differentiated products.
Cost-plus pricing requires an accurate calculation of all overhead costs.
A high initial price can deter potential customers if the value is not clear.

quiz.say: A company launches a revolutionary new solar-powered gadget at a very high price, expecting to lower it later.
quiz.why: This pattern of high to low pricing matches the definition of skimming.

wrong.0: This is not one of the three core strategies taught today.
wrong.2: Penetration suggests starting low to capture volume, not starting high.
wrong.3: Cost-plus only considers costs plus a fixed profit, not a strategic price drop.

quiz.say: A bakery sets its bread price by adding a fixed profit of two dollars to the total cost of flour, yeast, and labor.
quiz.why: This method directly calculates price by adding a fixed profit amount to the total cost.

wrong.1: Skimming requires setting the price based on perceived value, not just cost.
wrong.2: Penetration requires setting the price low to gain market share, not based on cost.
wrong.3: While related, the problem describes a fixed cost calculation, not perceived value.

quiz.say: A new streaming service enters a saturated market by offering its first three months for just one dollar.
quiz.show: Low price to gain many users.
quiz.why: Starting with a very low price is the core goal of penetration pricing.

wrong.0: Skimming would suggest starting with a very high price for novelty.
wrong.1: Cost-plus would set the price based on the service's operational costs.
wrong.2: Premium pricing suggests high value, which is the opposite of the stated low price.
